subject: Climate & Environment
title: Extended Producer Responsibility
description: A micro-lesson that makes Extended Producer Responsibility usable.

hook.text: Should the company that makes the packaging also pay to clean it up? More countries say yes.

buildup.text: Extended Producer Responsibility makes manufacturers fund the collection and recycling of their products.

discovery.text: Europe pioneered EPR in the 1990s. It dramatically increased packaging recycling rates.

twist.text: When companies pay for waste, they design less wasteful packaging — the incentive aligns.

climax.text: Over 400 EPR programs now exist worldwide. The UN plastic treaty may make them mandatory.

punchline.text: When the bill goes to the maker, the mess gets smaller.

quiz.question: What does Extended Producer Responsibility require?
options: Manufacturers fund waste collection and recycling

details.summary: Extended producer responsibility makes manufacturers responsible for the entire lifecycle of their products, including end-of-life collection and recycling.
details.whyItMatters: EPR shifts the cost of waste management from taxpayers to the companies that create the waste. This financial incentive drives manufacturers to design more recyclable and longer-lasting products.
takeaways: Producers pay for collection and recycling of their products
EPR incentivizes design for recyclability and durability
It has sharply increased recycling rates where implemented

faq.question: How does EPR work in practice?
faq.answer: Producers pay fees to compliance organizations based on the volume and type of products they sell. These organizations fund collection, sorting, and recycling infrastructure. Fees are higher for hard-to-recycle materials, incentivizing design changes.

faq.question: Which countries have the strongest EPR programs?
faq.answer: Germany pioneered packaging EPR in 1991. The EU now mandates EPR for packaging, electronics, and batteries. South Korea, Japan, and Canada also have robust programs. Coverage and effectiveness vary, with the best systems achieving recycling rates above 70 percent.
